Not nearly as good as Sora. Google missed this train, big time.

The demo videos are pretty neat and would have impressed four months earlier, but they are underwhelming next to the Sora demo, especially coming from Google, which owns the largest video collection in the world.

Shots are only a few seconds long and mostly slow-motion or slow panning, apparently cherry-picked to avoid hard movement. The one comparable fast cyberpunk clip 'looks crazy inconsistent', unlike Sora's real-speed walking videos.
Many of the samples shown fail to fully conform to their prompts, with lots of specifics missing. Credit to Google for being transparent about it.

GPT-4o shipped while Veo got a waitlist. Users called it a half-baked release unavailable in most countries, with confusing Veo vs VisionFX sign-up messaging and repeated sign-in prompts just to see a demo.

Veo 3: 'Blown away at how well the audio/video matches up, and the dialogue is better sounding / on-par with dedicated voice models.' Another user said the audio integration, covering both sounds and voices, makes a huge difference.
'Ehh, really for 20$. Break dancers with no music, people just pop in and out?' The user questioned how anyone would use this for a commercial application.

Professional tools now feel well ahead of open source. Wan and Hunyuan are solid, but the latest from Google and Runway feel 'a league above', with editing tools (prompting motion, cuts, weaving in audio) as the main differentiator. Still one or two generations off, though.
Doesn't look better than early Sora demos. The output is still smooth, shiny and robotic, unmistakably AI-generated.
Questioned Google's rater comparison: Veo samples were 8s while most competitors' were 5s. Raters might simply prefer longer videos, so Veo 2 output should have been trimmed to 5s for a fair test.

Winning 2:1 in preference over Sora Turbo is impressive and it may emulate physics slightly better, but it shares Sora's limitations: legs swap in the ice skating video and the beekeeper's jar pops up with unnatural acceleration.
The skateboarding video is wildly unrealistic whenever he performs a trick, with morphing body parts, though some other videos look incredibly believable.

Got preview access. For 'a pelican riding a bicycle along a coastal path', two of the outputs actually showed a pelican riding a bicycle; others had it running, perched on a stationary bike, or wearing a weird helmet. All were better than what Sora produced.
Several users said the Veo 2 announcement page crashed or struggled: it kept reloading on Brave iOS, crashed Chrome on iPad, and crashed the browser on iPhone.
Impressed that something as computationally expensive as 8-second video generation is available in Gemini and Whisk, not just through a paid API.
Tried it after 'Try it now!': entered a video prompt and literally nothing happened, it just went back to the prompt.

Veo 2 content moderation blocked a cartoon of the user drinking coffee and talking. Another user said moderation keeps blocking fun videos of their kid as a superhero, calling it incredibly frustrating.
Warning: burned through $48 in GCP credit making 12 eight-second videos with Veo 2.
Whisk (with Veo 2) redraws the entire image, so the video barely resembles the source picture.

Even the curated 'Glacial Cavern' demo misses the prompt: the candy figures are in the foreground instead of within the ice walls. Great if exactness doesn't matter, frustrating when an important detail is wrong.
